## Austin HVAC Warm-Air Troubleshooting Snapshot
A 9-year-old central system that blows warm air intermittently, especially in the afternoon, often points to a heat-load, airflow, or control issue rather than a full system failure. With a **$600 repair budget**, focus first on low-cost checks that can be done safely.

## Ranked Causes and Troubleshooting Checklist
| Rank | Likely cause | Why it fits | What to check now | Typical fix cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Thermostat settings or sensor drift | Intermittent warm air can happen if the thermostat is misreading room temperature or switching modes oddly | Confirm **Cool** mode, fan on **Auto**, batteries good, setpoint not too close to room temp | Low |
| 2 | Dirty condenser coil or blocked outdoor airflow | Afternoon heat in Austin can push a marginal system over the edge | Clear leaves/debris, check 2–3 ft around outdoor unit, look for visible dirt on coil | Low to moderate |
| 3 | Restricted indoor airflow | Reduced airflow can make the system feel warm or cycle poorly | Check supply vents open, return grilles unobstructed, filter seated correctly, weak airflow from registers | Low |
| 4 | Low refrigerant charge or small leak | Intermittent cooling and worse performance during peak heat are common signs | Look for ice on refrigerant lines or indoor coil, hissing, or oily residue near lines | Moderate to high |
| 5 | Failing capacitor or contactor | Electrical parts can work sometimes and fail more when hot | Outdoor unit not starting reliably, humming, fan stops, hard starts | Moderate |
| 6 | Compressor overheating or weakening | A 9-year-old system can still run but lose cooling capacity under afternoon load | Outdoor unit shuts off, restarts later, warm air after long run times | High |
| 7 | Duct leakage or attic heat gain | Afternoon worsening can happen when hot attic air overwhelms leaky ducts | Check for uneven room temps, hot attic ducts, weak far-room airflow | Moderate to high |
| 8 | Aging compressor or major refrigerant-side issue | Less common, but more serious if the system is losing capacity progressively | Repeated warm air, long run times, high electric bills, frequent service calls | High |

### Troubleshooting Checklist
- Confirm thermostat is set to **Cool** and fan to **Auto**.
- Lower the setpoint by 3–5 degrees and see whether the outdoor unit starts normally.
- Replace or inspect the filter again if it is visibly dusty or warped.
- Make sure all supply vents are open and return vents are not blocked by furniture.
- Go outside and clear grass, leaves, and debris from the condenser.
- Verify the outdoor fan is spinning and the unit is blowing warm air out the top.
- Check for ice on the indoor refrigerant line, evaporator coil access, or outdoor line set.
- Note whether the problem happens only during the hottest part of the day.
- Listen for clicking, humming, short cycling, or repeated shutdowns.
- If safe, check the breaker once; if it trips again, stop and call a pro.

## What to Do First With a $600 Budget
- **Best low-cost path:** thermostat check, airflow check, condenser cleaning, and a technician visit if needed.
- **Most likely repair within budget:** capacitor, contactor, drain/airflow correction, or minor control issue.
- **Possible budget stretch:** refrigerant leak detection or coil cleaning may fit, but a major leak or compressor issue usually will not.

## When to Call an HVAC Technician
Call a technician soon if any of these are true:
- The outdoor unit runs but the air stays warm after 10–15 minutes.
- You see **ice**, hear **hissing**, or notice **oily residue** near refrigerant lines.
- The outdoor unit struggles to start, hums, or trips the breaker.
- Airflow is weak even with clean vents and a good filter.
- The issue is getting worse week by week.
- The system is short-cycling or shutting off more often in afternoon heat.

Call immediately if:
- The breaker keeps tripping.
- The indoor coil is frozen.
- You smell burning or see electrical damage.
- The system makes loud grinding or metal-on-metal noises.
